title: Did Early Humans Keep Souvenirs 500,000 Years Ago?
paragraphs: The urge to hold on to a souvenir feels distinctly modern, yet a paper in Evolutionary Anthropology argues that its roots may reach back roughly half a million years. Researchers at Tel Aviv University and Oxford University propose that early humans in what is now Israel were already gathering objects for their personal meaning rather than their usefulness.

The case rests on a handful of archaeological patterns. At Qesem Cave, small, colourful pebbles had been carried in from elsewhere with no identifiable function, and old flint tools that had weathered before being collected were kept with much of their original surface intact. In the Sakhnin Valley, handaxes were deliberately shaped so that fossils or unusual geological features sat at the centre of the stone. The authors contend that such items served as external memory devices, anchoring recollections of particular places and helping people separate what they had lived through from what they had merely been told, a distinction that could underpin trust and cooperation. Co-author Ran Barkai also links the shift to the decline of large game such as elephants, which forced groups to learn new hunting grounds.

Crucially, the authors frame all this as a hypothesis, not a demonstration. A pebble's meaning cannot be recovered from the pebble alone, so the argument will stand or fall on whether further finds repeat the pattern across other sites and periods.

questions.q: What do the authors think the collected objects did for their owners?
questions.a: They acted as external memory devices, anchoring recollections of places and experiences.

questions.q: How does Ran Barkai connect the behaviour to the environment?
questions.a: He links it to the decline of large game such as elephants, which forced people to learn new hunting grounds.
Further finds showing the same pattern at other sites and periods.
